The logs show no kernel panic or reboot on combo between 2005-11-15 and 2005-12-01. What does show up is a long run of kernel 'Out of Memory: Killed process ... (httpd).' lines, peaking on 2005-11-21, plus two syslogd restarts that look like routine rotation rather than reboots.
Scope: Dataset linux, node combo (the only node), 2005-11-15 00:00:00 → 2005-12-01 00:00:00. Filters: pattern_id 700495 and keyword searches. The panic and restart searches were not truncated; the OOM line search returned a sample of 1 of 6709 lines; one search for 'Kernel command line' covered 2005-10-01 → 2006-01-15.
A search for panic, 'kernel panic' or Oops in the window returned 0 matches.
The only restart-type lines in the window are 2 syslogd '1.4.1: restart.' lines on node combo, at 2005-11-20 04:09:36 and 2005-11-27 04:06:31.
cupsd shutdown/startup lines sit just before each syslogd restart: 'cupsd shutdown succeeded' 2005-11-20 04:08:59 and 'cupsd startup succeeded' 04:09:08; 'cupsd shutdown succeeded' 2005-11-27 04:06:06 and 'cupsd startup succeeded' 04:06:17.
Around the 2005-11-20 04:09:36 restart: before = 'session opened for user cyrus by (uid=0)' (04:08:53), 'session closed for user cyrus' (04:08:54), then the cupsd lines; at = syslogd '1.4.1: restart.'; after = logrotate 'ALERT exited abnormally with [1]' at 04:09:37.
The nearest line before that window was a kernel 'Out of Memory: Killed process 16185 (httpd).' at 2005-11-20 03:38:24 (1872.0 seconds before the restart). The nearest line after was 'Out of Memory: Killed process 16845 (httpd).' at 05:05:27 (3351.0 seconds after).
The search for 'Kernel command line' (a boot-time kernel line) across 2005-10-01 → 2006-01-15 found 2 matches, at 2005-10-25 10:08:47 and 2005-12-06 12:22:57, both outside the period the question asks about.
The recurring kernel pattern 700495 'Out of Memory: Killed process N (httpd).' has 6709 log lines in the window on 1 node, first at 2005-11-15 04:30:29 and last at 2005-11-30 13:56:48 (the last line is 'Out of Memory: Killed process 8846 (httpd).').
Daily OOM-kill log lines rose from 88 on 2005-11-15 to 1750 on 2005-11-21, then fell to 77 on 2005-11-27 and rose again to 727 on 2005-11-29. The pattern continues after the window, with 960 on 2005-12-03 and 1162 on 2005-12-04.
Kernel lines were 8051 of 8675 total log lines in the window.
The OOM kills come in bursts with a new httpd PID each time. Example: 'Out of Memory: Killed process 11722 (httpd).' at 2005-11-18 23:55:38, then 'Out of Memory: Killed process 11723 (httpd).' at 2005-11-19 00:00:34, then 'Out of Memory: Killed process 11724 (httpd).' at 00:10:28.
The earliest boot in the corpus (2005-06-09 06:06:20) logged 'Memory: 125312k/129720k available (1540k kernel code, 3860k reserved, 599k data, 144k init, 0k highmem)'.
Hypothesis: The reported 'panics' may actually be httpd being repeatedly OOM-killed on a small-memory host (about 125 MB at boot), making the machine appear to crash or hang. The 2005-11-20 04:09 and 2005-11-27 04:06 syslogd restarts may be routine scheduled log rotation (cups restart, then logrotate) rather than reboots. Would confirm: Check for console, serial or other host logs showing real panics or reboots, and for 'Linux version' or 'Kernel command line' boot lines in the window (none were found). Compare the restart times with the logrotate/cron schedule and with httpd memory use, MaxClients and swap.
Unknown: Whether the host actually panicked or rebooted: these logs contain no panic or Oops lines and no boot lines in the window.
Unknown: The root cause of the httpd memory exhaustion, such as traffic, a leak or a misconfiguration.
Unknown: What triggered the OOM growth starting around 2005-11-19 to 2005-11-21.
Unknown: Customer impact and downtime are not in the logs.
Unknown: Whether panics were logged somewhere outside this dataset, such as on the console or a different log host.

new.text:
The logs do not show a kernel panic or a reboot on combo between 2005-11-15 and 2005-12-01. What they do show is a new burst of kernel Out of Memory kills (pattern 700495) starting 2005-11-15 04:30:29, plus page-allocation failures with call traces from 2005-11-21 12:41:10. The only 'shutting down for system reboot' line is on 2005-12-06, outside your window.
Scope: Dataset linux (one host, combo). Searches covered 2005-11-15 00:00:00 → 2005-12-01 00:00:00, with one wider search over 2005-11-01 → 2005-12-15. Pattern history covers the whole dataset. Counts for patterns 700495 and 700499 are exact totals, but only sample rows were returned. The facet output was truncated (24 of 8675 log lines shown). The context result around 2005-11-21 12:41:10 was also truncated.
A prefix search for 'panic' on linux in 2005-11-15 → 2005-12-01 returned 0 matches.
A search for 'syslogd 1.4.1', klogd, 'Linux version', 'Kernel command line' and 'BIOS-provided' in 2005-11-15 → 2005-12-01 returned 0 matches, so no boot-banner lines were found in the window.
The wider search (2005-11-01 → 2005-12-15, 43 matches, 1 node) found within your window only two weekly pairs of 'cupsd shutdown succeeded' followed by 'syslogd 1.4.1: restart.': 2005-11-20 04:08:59 / 04:09:36 and 2005-11-27 04:06:06 / 04:06:31. The first 'shutting down for system reboot' line is 2005-12-06 12:20:08, outside the window.
Kernel lines were 8051 of 8675 log lines in the window. Pattern 700495 accounts for 6709 log lines and pattern 700499 for 998.
Pattern 700495 ('Out of Memory: Killed process <N> <*>', component kernel, 1 node) has 6709 log lines in the window, first 2005-11-15 04:30:29 and last 2005-11-30 13:56:48. The first lines read 'Out of Memory: Killed process 28473 (httpd).' at 04:30:29 and 'Out of Memory: Killed process 28474 (httpd).' at 04:35:29.
Pattern 700495 is new: bursts_before is 0 and lines_before is 0 as of 2005-11-15. Over the whole dataset it has 10404 log lines in 133 bursts, active 4 weeks, from 2005-11-15T04:30:29 to 2005-12-09T04:58:54. The median gap between bursts is 1:14:50.
Daily log lines for pattern 700495 are 0 on every day up to 2005-11-14, then 88 on 2005-11-15 (3 bursts started), 848 on 2005-11-20 (9 bursts), 1750 on 2005-11-21 (8 bursts) and 727 on 2005-11-29 (6 bursts).
Pattern 700499 (kernel stack-trace lines such as ' [<0212ebf3>] __alloc_pages+0x274/0x281') has 998 log lines on 1 node, from 2005-11-21 12:41:10 to 2005-11-29 04:43:48.
Timeline around 2005-11-21 12:41:10. Before: the nearest earlier line outside the context window is 2005-11-21 12:39:03 on combo, 'Out of Memory: Killed process 28853 (python).', 127.0 s earlier. Inside the window, OOM kills run roughly every 5-6 s, e.g. 12:40:07 'Out of Memory: Killed process 28874 (httpd).' and 12:40:57 'Out of Memory: Killed process 28852 (mrtg).' At: 12:41:10 'httpd: page allocation failure. order:0, mode:0xd2', then 'Call Trace:' with ' [<0212ebf3>] __alloc_pages+0x274/0x281', ' [<0213d341>] read_swap_cache_async+0x41/0x84' and ' [<02135dee>] swapin_readahead+0x2c/0x47'. After: 12:41:12 'httpd: page allocation failure. order:0, mode:0xd2' again, and the nearest later line outside the window is 2005-11-21 14:15:23 on combo, 'Out of Memory: Killed process 28886 (httpd).', 5653.0 s later.
Killed processes in the sampled context include httpd, sendmail, mrtg and python. Everything is on one node (combo), so it is local to this host.
Hypothesis: A possible cause is memory exhaustion on combo: the Out of Memory kills, swap-in call traces and order:0 page-allocation failures point to memory and swap exhaustion, possibly driven by httpd, sendmail, mrtg or python workloads. If hard resets were ever triggered, the memory pressure may be their trigger. Would confirm: Check memory and swap history (sar -r / sar -B) from 2005-11-15 onward, httpd process counts or MaxClients and the mrtg schedule around 2005-11-15 04:30, and any change deployed just before that time. Also look for a gap in combo's log lines followed by boot messages.
Unknown: Whether any kernel panic occurred: these logs contain no 'panic' line in the window, and a panic that killed the host might not have been written to /var/log/messages at all.
Unknown: Whether the host actually rebooted between 2005-11-15 and 2005-12-01: the only restarts found are the weekly cups/syslogd pairs, and no boot-banner lines were found in the window.
Unknown: The root cause of the memory pressure, and which process or change started it.
Unknown: Downtime or customer impact: not in the logs.
Next step: Check for log silence on node combo. Query all log lines for 2005-11-15 → 2005-12-01 ordered by time, look for multi-minute gaps (especially around the busiest OOM days, 2005-11-20 and 2005-11-21), and see what is logged right after each gap. — Without 'panic' or boot-banner matches, a gap followed by startup lines is the only way these logs could show a hard reset.
Next step: Run pattern_history and precursors for pattern 700499 (the page-allocation-failure traces) and check which components log just before the first OOM kill at 2005-11-15 04:30:29. — 700495 appears with no earlier history (0 bursts before 2005-11-15), so something changed at that time.
Next step: Inspect the host's memory, swap and httpd configuration and process counts, and any console or serial logs and the hardware watchdog, which could capture a panic that syslog did not. — The OOM kills touch httpd, sendmail, mrtg and python, and syslog may not capture a real panic.

new.text:
This looks new, not long-standing: the 'Out of Memory: Killed process' pattern first appeared on 2005-11-15 and logged 133 bursts in the window against 0 in the prior two months. It was large on this single host (10404 log lines), and the logs cannot say what it cost or who it affected.
Scope: Dataset linux (one host, combo, linux-ops). Period 2005-11-01 to 2006-01-01, compared with 2005-09-01 to 2005-11-01. Filter: problem patterns only (40 candidates; the priority table shows the top 10, so the results are truncated). The weekly memory-keyword trend covers the whole corpus, 2005-06-09 to 2006-01-26.
Team roll-up for linux-ops: 40 problem patterns, 331 bursts (176 in the previous period, change 155), 11294 log lines.
The pattern 'Out of Memory: Killed process <N> <*>' was first seen 2005-11-15 04:30:29. It had 133 bursts in the window and 0 in the previous period. It accounts for 10404 log lines on 1 node across 4 weeks.
The OOM kill log lines peaked at 1750 on 2005-11-21 and ran from 2005-11-15 to 2005-12-09 04:58:54.
Memory-keyword log lines per week were 1667, 3271, 4178 and 1294 for the weeks starting 2005-11-14, 2005-11-21, 2005-11-28 and 2005-12-05. Before that, no week had more than 12 such lines. The weeks starting 2005-12-12 through 2006-01-16 had 0.
Related memory patterns were also new in November: httpd page allocation failures (14, 10 and 8 bursts), sendmail page allocation failures (4 bursts), and 'VM: killing process httpd' (14 bursts) and 'VM: killing process sendmail' (2 bursts).
Across the whole dataset, problem bursts per week were 104 in the week of 2005-11-21, against 7 in each of the weeks of 2005-12-12, 2005-12-19 and 2005-12-26. The overall reading is 'worsening' (1042 bursts in total).
1. Kernel out-of-memory killer terminating processes (new since 2005-11-15) — owner linux-ops — 133 bursts, 0 in previous period (change 133), 1 node, 4 weeks active, 10404 log lines, score 97.5 — Decide whether to fund a capacity and memory-limit review of this server and add memory alerting.
2. SSH authentication failures (long-standing, not a memory issue; the model judged it 'not a problem') — owner linux-ops — 25 bursts, 20 in previous period (change 5), 1 node, 6 weeks active, score 94.9 — Decide whether this recurring noise warrants attention. It ranks high on persistence, not because of the memory problem.
3. Kernel 'VM: killing process httpd' (web server killed under memory pressure, new) — owner linux-ops — 14 bursts, 0 in previous period (change 14), 1 node, 3 weeks active, 26 log lines, score 89.1 — Ask linux-ops whether the web service needs a resource limit or a restart policy, and whether it needs to be moved or resized.
Hypothesis: A change around 2005-11-15 (a workload or configuration change, or a memory leak in httpd) may have exhausted memory, because the page allocation failures and kills involve httpd and sendmail. Would confirm: Check change records and deployments around 2005-11-15, per-process memory and swap history, and whether the OOM kills stopped after a fix or reboot around 2005-12-09.
Unknown: Cost, downtime and customer impact are not in these logs.
Unknown: Root cause is not in these logs.
Unknown: These logs cannot show whether the OOM kills stopped because of a fix or because of a reboot or a change in load; no OOM log lines appear after 2005-12-09.
Unknown: The January 2006 rise in overall problem bursts is outside the requested window and was not analysed.
Next step: Review memory configuration and httpd/sendmail memory use on the combo host, and what changed around 2005-11-15; report back. — The OOM pattern is new, with 133 bursts against 0 before, concentrated on one node.
Next step: Decide whether to fund memory monitoring and alerting that records metrics, not only log lines. — The logs cannot show cost, downtime or customer impact, so impact data has to come from other sources.

SELECT s.b AS bucket_start, count(x.t) AS bursts FROM generate_series(date_trunc('week', TIMESTAMP '2005-06-09 00:00:00'), TIMESTAMP '2006-03-01 00:00:00', interval '7 days') s(b) LEFT JOIN (SELECT b.start_ts AS t FROM bursts b JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = b.dataset AND p.pattern_id = b.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = p.dataset AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = p.dataset AND j.pattern_id = p.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 AND p.problem_lines > 0 AND b.dataset = 'linux' AND b.start_ts >= '2005-06-09 00:00:00' AND b.start_ts < '2006-03-01 00:00:00') x ON date_trunc('week', x.t) = s.b GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

SELECT team, round(regr_slope(n, i), 3) AS slope, sum(n) AS bursts FROM (SELECT t.team, s.i, count(x.t) AS n FROM (SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY b) - 1 AS i, b FROM generate_series(date_trunc('week', TIMESTAMP '2005-06-09 00:00:00'), TIMESTAMP '2006-03-01 00:00:00', interval '7 days') s(b)) s CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT coalesce(o.team, 'unowned') AS team FROM bursts b JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = b.dataset AND p.pattern_id = b.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = p.dataset AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = p.dataset AND j.pattern_id = p.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 AND p.problem_lines > 0 AND b.dataset = 'linux' AND b.start_ts >= '2005-06-09 00:00:00' AND b.start_ts < '2006-03-01 00:00:00') t LEFT JOIN (SELECT b.start_ts AS t, coalesce(o.team, 'unowned') AS team FROM bursts b JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = b.dataset AND p.pattern_id = b.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = p.dataset AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = p.dataset AND j.pattern_id = p.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 AND p.problem_lines > 0 AND b.dataset = 'linux' AND b.start_ts >= '2005-06-09 00:00:00' AND b.start_ts < '2006-03-01 00:00:00') x ON date_trunc('week', x.t) = s.b AND x.team = t.team GROUP BY 1, 2) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY bursts DESC

coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2005-11-01 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'linux' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'linux' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'linux' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND now.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ), inputs AS ( SELECT *, round(weeks_active::DOUBLE / 9, 3) AS persistence, round(problem_lines::DOUBLE / lines, 3) AS problem_share, p_problem AS severity_input FROM base ), ranked AS ( SELECT *, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY bursts) AS pr_frequency, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY change) AS pr_trend, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY nodes) AS pr_spread, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY persistence) AS pr_persistence, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY severity_input) AS pr_severity FROM inputs ) SELECT *, round(100 * (0.3 * pr_frequency + 0.2 * pr_trend + 0.25 * pr_spread + 0.15 * pr_persistence + 0.1 * pr_severity), 1) AS score FROM ranked ORDER BY score DESC, bursts DESC, pattern_id

coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2005-11-01 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'linux' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'linux' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'linux' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND now.problem_lines > 0 AND coalesce(j.p_problem, 0) < 0.5 ) SELECT pattern_id, template, component, team, bursts, lines, nodes, p_problem, kind FROM base ORDER BY bursts DESC, pattern_id LIMIT 3

On 2017-12-15 sshd-16980 on node LabSZ was a password login for the valid user zachary from 218.17.80.182. It had two failed passwords, then an accepted password at 10:39:04, and the session closed at 18:40:58. The logs fit a returning user who mistyped a password, not a brute-force attack, but they cannot prove who was at the keyboard.
Scope: Dataset ssh, node LabSZ, request_id sshd-16980 on 2017-12-15 00:00:00 → 2017-12-16 00:00:00. Wider checks used entity ip:218.17.80.182 and the text "zachary" over the whole corpus. The entity search was not truncated. The "zachary" text search was truncated to 30 of 34 matches. The ±10 min node context on 2017-12-15 was not truncated.
On 2017-12-15 request sshd-16980 has 6 log lines on 1 node (LabSZ), first at 2017-12-15 10:38:55 and last at 2017-12-15 18:40:58.
Login phase, verbatim. 10:38:55 'pam_unix(sshd:auth): authentication failure; logname= uid=0 euid=0 tty=ssh ruser= rhost=218.17.80.182  user=zachary'. 10:38:57 'Failed password for zachary from 218.17.80.182 port 60110 ssh2'. 10:39:03 'Failed password for zachary from 218.17.80.182 port 60110 ssh2'. 10:39:04 'Accepted password for zachary from 218.17.80.182 port 60110 ssh2'. 10:39:04 'pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user zachary by (uid=0)'.
The login phase is 5 log lines over 9.0 s with 0 problem lines. The failed attempts all used the same port 60110 and ended in 'Accepted password'.
After the login, the only later line in this request that day is 'pam_unix(sshd:session): session closed for user zachary' at 2017-12-15 18:40:58.
The request_id sshd-16980 is reused: it splits into 6 sessions (quiet gaps > 3600 s), and this was session 3 of 6. The nearest earlier line of sshd-16980 is 2017-12-12 05:11:00 'Connection closed by 183.238.178.195 [preauth]'. The nearest later line is 2017-12-30 07:57:40 'pam_unix(sshd:auth): authentication failure; ... rhost=139.219.191.138  user=root'. Those are different sessions with different source IPs.
Before, on node LabSZ: the closest earlier line is 2017-12-15 10:33:17 'Received disconnect from 52.80.34.196: 11: Bye Bye [preauth]' (request sshd-16977, an 'Invalid user sugon' attempt). After: the next line is 2017-12-15 10:46:08 'Invalid user butter from 185.165.29.140' (request sshd-17102). Both come from other IPs and other requests, so the event is local to the connection.
IP 218.17.80.182 has 20 log lines on 1 node, from 2017-12-11 16:48:51 to 2017-12-21 14:07:31. All of them are for user zachary.
The same sequence recurs on earlier days: on 2017-12-12 (sshd-29120), 2017-12-13 (sshd-5459) and 2017-12-14 (sshd-9262) an 'authentication failure' line, one 'Failed password' line, then 'Accepted password' from 218.17.80.182. It repeats on 2017-12-19 (sshd-10647) and 2017-12-21 (sshd-19308). The 2017-12-15 connection had two 'Failed password' lines, not one.
The 'zachary' text search shows each of those days ending with a 'session closed for user zachary' line, for example 2017-12-14 21:49:46 and 2017-12-19 18:00:24.
Hypothesis: Possible cause: a legitimate user (zachary) mistyped the password once more than usual and then logged in. The pattern is not new. The attempts come from one IP, which is repeatedly seen on other days, and the correct password was accepted within 9.0 s. Would confirm: Confirm that 218.17.80.182 belongs to zachary (VPN or office range, asset or IAM records). Check that nothing else from that IP targeted other usernames. Check zachary's shell or audit history for 2017-12-15 10:39–18:40.
Hypothesis: Possible alternative: the failed attempts were a guess at zachary's password by someone using the same IP (shared NAT or a compromised account). This is less likely, since there were only two failures before a success and the IP shows the same one-failure pattern on other days. Would confirm: Look for logins by zachary from other IPs and for any unusual activity inside the session. Check whether the password was recently changed or exposed.
Unknown: Whether the person at 218.17.80.182 was the real zachary. The logs show only authentication events, not identity.
Unknown: What zachary did during the session from 10:39:04 to 18:40:58. The logs hold only open and close lines.
Unknown: Why the first attempt always logs an 'authentication failure' before the accepted login on these days. It could be client behaviour such as a key or empty-password try, but the logs do not say.
Unknown: Customer impact, cost or downtime are not in these logs.
Next step: Run search_logs on dataset ssh with entity ip:218.17.80.182, excluding user zachary, to confirm the IP never tried other usernames. Then compare the source IP and port 60110 with the VPN or firewall logs for 2017-12-15 10:38:55. — All 20 log lines for this IP are for zachary, but only the ssh dataset was checked. Network or VPN logs can show whether it is zachary's usual source.
Next step: Ask zachary or check IAM records whether he logged in from 218.17.80.182 on 2017-12-15 around 10:39 and held the session until 18:40, and whether his password was changed or leaked recently. — Only the account owner can settle real user versus compromised credentials; the logs show a successful login after 2 failed passwords.
Next step: Inspect the LabSZ auth log and shell or audit history for zachary between 2017-12-15 10:39:04 and 18:40:58. — The ssh log has only session-open and session-close lines (131637 and 139432), so activity during the session is not visible.

new.text:
These logs show heavy password-guessing against root and invalid users in the first week of January 2018, but no successful root login: the search for "Accepted password for root" returned 0 log lines. They cannot confirm or rule out a root compromise, so security-ops should check the host directly first.
Scope: Dataset ssh (OpenSSH auth log, host LabSZ). Period 2018-01-01 to 2018-01-08 (log ends 2018-01-07 17:22:01), compared with 2017-12-25 to 2018-01-01. Filters: problem patterns only. The priority table is truncated (10 of 39 shown); the ranking below uses its top 3. Other results are not truncated.
Searching for "Accepted password for root" returned 0 log lines in 2018-01-01 to 2018-01-08 and 0 log lines across the whole dataset.
94 log lines in the window match "Accepted password" or "Accepted publickey" (any user). These logs do not break them down by user or source.
The 'failed password for root' watch fired: 102039 log lines in the window vs 13488 in the previous week, first seen 2018-01-01 00:12:30.
The 'too many auth failures' watch fired: 35318 log lines vs 1329 in the previous week. The 'break-in attempt' watch fired: 14881 log lines vs 1813.
Team roll-up: security-ops owns all 39 problem patterns, with 1207 bursts this week vs 478 the previous week (change 729) and 281388 log lines.
Across the 28-day dataset the daily problem-burst trend reads 'no clear change' (3750 bursts in total). Days with 0 bursts ran from 2017-12-24 to 2017-12-28.
1. Repeated 'Invalid user' login attempts from attacker IPs (username guessing) — owner security-ops — 108 bursts vs 37 the previous week (change 71); 1 node; 1 week active; 4340 log lines — Decide whether to fund and approve blocking or rate-limiting of repeat source IPs and disabling password logins on the internet-facing SSH server.
2. Failed password attempts for invalid users — owner security-ops — 108 bursts vs 37 the previous week (change 71); 1 node; 1 week active; 6130 log lines — Ask security-ops to confirm none of these source IPs later appear in a successful login, and to report back.
3. Invalid-user requests rejected before authentication (preauth) — owner security-ops — 108 bursts vs 37 the previous week (change 71); 1 node; 1 week active; 4340 log lines — Treat as part of the same attack wave. Decide on a rule or policy change for the exposed SSH server.
Hypothesis: If root was compromised, it may have happened by a route not matching 'Accepted password for root', such as a public-key login, another account followed by privilege escalation, or tampered logs. Would confirm: Break down the 94 accepted-login lines by user and source IP, and check the host itself (login history, authorized_keys, new accounts, file changes).
Hypothesis: The days with 0 problem bursts (2017-12-24 to 2017-12-28) may be a gap in log collection rather than a real lull. Would confirm: Compare raw log line counts per day for those dates.
Unknown: Whether root was actually compromised: these logs show attempts, not proof either way.
Unknown: Cost, downtime and customer impact are not in these logs.
Unknown: Root cause and the attackers' identity are not established by these logs.
Next step: Review the 94 accepted-login lines by user and source IP, including any root public-key logins, and run a host forensic check for persistence. — The logs show 0 'Accepted password for root' lines but heavy root guessing (102039 log lines), so only a host check can settle whether root was compromised.
Next step: Approve interim hardening: disable root and password SSH logins, and block or rate-limit repeat attacker IPs. — Problem bursts rose from 478 to 1207 week over week, and the top three patterns each show 108 bursts.
Next step: Check whether logs for 2017-12-24 to 2017-12-28 are missing. — 0 bursts per day in that stretch may hide earlier activity.

Yes. The Apache dataset has 1039 log lines on 2006-01-08 against a baseline rate of 1.286 per hour over the previous 7 days, and 965 of them are ERROR. Most of the errors are "File does not exist" for /var/www/html/awstats/awstats.pl. Three IPs account for the biggest bursts: 193.19.219.217, 61.134.40.151 and 218.106.165.188.
Scope: Dataset apache, 2006-01-08 00:00:00 → 2006-01-09 00:00:00, compared with 2006-01-01 00:00:00 → 2006-01-08 00:00:00 (7 windows of 24 h). Unit is log lines. The facet, IP list and search samples are truncated (IP list shows 15 of 27 values; samples show only a few rows), but the totals are complete. The error-pattern facet (ERROR only, 965 lines) is not truncated.
On 2006-01-08 the apache dataset has 1039 log lines (43.292 per hour). The previous 7 days have 216 log lines (1.286 per hour), a ratio of 33.7. The busiest baseline day had 89 log lines, and 0 baseline windows reached 1039 or more.
Of the 1039 log lines, 965 are ERROR and 74 are NOTICE. The httpd component accounts for 951 lines.
Among the ERROR lines (965), pattern 300021 has 599 log lines, 300033 has 132, 300042 has 129, 300020 has 42, and 300022 and 300023 have 22 each. There are 20 distinct error patterns.
Pattern 300021 is verbatim: "[client 193.19.219.217] File does not exist: /var/www/html/awstats/awstats.pl". Pattern 300033 is "[client 84.155.141.86] script not found or unable to stat: /var/www/cgi-bin/awstats.pl". Pattern 300020 is "[client 60.222.194.88] Directory index forbidden by rule: /var/www/html/".
Top client IPs by log lines: 193.19.219.217 has 253 (16:42:20 → 16:42:38), 61.134.40.151 has 233 (16:35:32 → 16:36:18), 218.106.165.188 has 198 (18:24:47 → 18:25:09). 27 distinct IPs appear in total.
Pattern 300033 runs from 2006-01-08 15:14:05 to 18:24:53 (132 log lines). Pattern 300042 ("script not found or unable to stat", no client in the message) runs from 15:14:06 to 18:25:05 (129 log lines).
Timeline for the 16:42:20 burst. Before: at 16:42:00 "[client 219.147.185.1] Directory index forbidden by rule: /var/www/html/". At: the 193.19.219.217 burst, with 8 identical awstats.pl lines inside the 16:42:20 second. After: more of the same lines at 16:42:21. The nearest earlier line outside the 5-minute window is 16:36:19, mod_jk2 NOTICE "mod_jk2 Shutting down", 361.0 s before the anchor. The nearest later line is 18:12:42, "[client 59.58.194.229] Directory index forbidden by rule: /var/www/html/", 5422.0 s after.
Timeline for the 15:14 burst from 84.155.141.86. Before: three "File does not exist ... awstats.pl" lines at 15:13:59. At 15:14:05: "[client 84.155.141.86] script not found or unable to stat: /var/www/cgi-bin/awstats.pl". Interleaved after it: "jk2_init() Can't find child 2725 in scoreboard", "workerEnv.init() ok /etc/httpd/conf/workers2.properties" and "mod_jk child init 1 -2". The nearest earlier line is 14:35:43 (Directory index forbidden, 2302.0 s before) and the nearest later line is 16:35:32 (4887.0 s after).
The facet returned no node values (node dimension lines 1039, share 1.0), and the search results show 0 distinct nodes. Node-level locality therefore cannot be read from these results.
Hypothesis: The spike may come from automated scanners probing for an awstats.pl script, with each IP sending a rapid burst of requests for a path that does not exist. The 15:14 burst also coincides with jk2/mod_jk child-init errors, which may be a side effect of Apache child processes being spawned under that request load. Would confirm: Check the Apache access log for those IPs and the awstats.pl paths (status codes, user agents). Check whether awstats exists on this host. Check whether the jk2_init / mod_jk errors also appear at other times, away from the bursts.
Unknown: Whether the same awstats.pl probing happened in the previous 7 days. Only line totals were compared, not pattern-level history.
Unknown: Which node produced the lines: node values are empty in these results.
Unknown: Whether any request succeeded, or what the response codes were. Only error-log lines are available here.
Unknown: Customer impact, downtime and cost are not in the logs.
Unknown: The root cause of the jk2_init / mod_jk child-init errors.

Pattern 300021 'File does not exist' accounts for 599 ERROR log lines (first 2006-01-08 02:12:47, last 2006-01-08 18:39:08). Pattern 300020 'Directory index forbidden by rule: /var/www/html/' accounts for 42 ERROR log lines (first 2006-01-08 00:13:38, last 2006-01-08 23:26:23).

132 ERROR log lines mention a client but are neither 'File does not exist' nor 'Directory index forbidden', between 2006-01-08 15:14:05 and 2006-01-08 18:24:53. The earliest ones read '[client 84.155.141.86] script not found or unable to stat: /var/www/cgi-bin/awstats.pl', and 61.134.40.151 sent the same kind of request at 16:35:33.

Timeline start: the first line of the day is 2006-01-08 00:13:38 '[client 60.222.194.88] Directory index forbidden by rule: /var/www/html/', followed by further 'Directory index forbidden' lines from 219.110.187.57, 221.232.176.105 and 198.70.193.2 up to 01:26:30.

At 2006-01-08 02:12:47 nine identical lines '[client 83.16.14.142] File does not exist: /var/www/html/sumthin' were logged in the same second. They were followed at 02:12:47 by NOTICE 'jk2_init() Found child 30096 in scoreboard slot 9' and NOTICE 'workerEnv.init() ok /etc/httpd/conf/workers2.properties'. Client 83.16.14.142 has 23 log lines between 02:12:47 and 02:12:49.

Client 218.106.165.188 has 198 log lines between 2006-01-08 18:24:47 and 2006-01-08 18:25:09. They start with '[client 218.106.165.188] File does not exist: /var/www/html/awstats/awstats.pl' and continue with repeated xmlrpc and xmlsrv probes.

Client 70.113.52.160 has 13 log lines between 2006-01-08 18:39:04 and 2006-01-08 18:39:09. They include probes such as '/var/www/html/scripts/root.exe', '/var/www/html/msadc' and '/var/www/html/scripts/..%5c..'.
The last line of the day is 2006-01-08 23:26:23 '[client 68.145.116.232] Directory index forbidden by rule: /var/www/html/'. The previous line, from 209.249.137.111, is at 22:38:21.
NOTICE lines matching 'Found child' or 'workerEnv.init()' number 44, first at 2006-01-08 02:12:47 and last at 2006-01-08 18:24:51.

hypotheses.statement: The spike may be automated vulnerability scanning of the web server by several external clients. The probed paths (awstats, xmlrpc, root.exe, msadc, directory traversal strings) are typical scanner targets, and each burst produces many 'File does not exist' errors in seconds.
hypotheses.would_confirm: Group the day's ERROR lines by client IP (count_by or facet on the ip entity) and check whether a few IPs account for most of the 599 'File does not exist' lines. Compare with the access log for status codes and user agents.

hypotheses.statement: The jk2_init / workerEnv.init() NOTICE lines right after the 02:12:47 burst may reflect Apache starting a new child process (mod_jk2 worker initialisation) while serving the burst, rather than a separate fault.
hypotheses.would_confirm: Check whether each 'Found child' NOTICE follows an ERROR burst, using precursors for pattern 300016 and 300018, and check the apache error log for restart or child-spawn messages around 02:12:47.

unknowns: Whether the requests were malicious, and whether any of them succeeded: these logs show only error lines, not the HTTP responses.
Which clients sent the most errors across the whole day: only samples and per-IP counts for four IPs were retrieved.
Why 2006-01-02 to 2006-01-05 have 0 log lines (quiet server or missing log data) is not established.
Customer impact, downtime or cost are not in the logs.
Node-level spread cannot be assessed because the logs carry no node (distinct_nodes 0).

next_steps.action: Run a count_by / facet on client IP entity for dataset apache, 2006-01-08 00:00:00 → 2006-01-09 00:00:00, severity ERROR, to rank the clients that sent the 965 errors.
next_steps.why: The sampled rows show 218.106.165.188 (198 log lines), 83.16.14.142 (23) and 70.113.52.160 (13), but the full ranking of senders is not in the evidence.

next_steps.action: Run the same count_by with pattern_id 300021 and 300020 per hour for 2006-01-08 and 2006-01-09, and run precursors for pattern 300016 / 300018.
next_steps.why: This shows whether the 763 log lines on 2006-01-09 are the same scan pattern, and whether the child-init NOTICE lines follow the bursts.

next_steps.action: Inspect the web server's access log and config for the probed paths (/var/www/html/awstats, xmlrpc, scripts/root.exe) and consider blocking or rate-limiting the repeating source IPs.
next_steps.why: Confirms whether any probe returned a non-404 response, which the error log cannot show.

Team roll-up of problem bursts: coordination-platform 35 bursts across 7 problem patterns and client-connectivity 30 bursts across 4 problem patterns, 65 bursts in total. storage-persistence does not appear.

1. 2. 'Cannot open channel to <N> at election address' (quorum peer connection failures) — owner coordination-platform — 8 bursts, change 8 versus 0 in the previous period, 5 weeks active, 2584 log lines, score 86.4 — Ask coordination-platform to confirm whether the election-address failures are ongoing, since the pattern was active in all 5 weeks.
3. 'Unexpected Exception:' in NIOServerCnxn — owner client-connectivity — 9 bursts, change 9 versus 0 in the previous period, 2 weeks active, 27 log lines, score 82.7 — Fold into the client-connectivity review with rank 1; fund it only if rank 1 does not explain it.

In these logs the storage-persistence team's issues were not serious: all 284 of its log lines were INFO, and none of its patterns qualified as a problem pattern. Their fixes should not come first; client-connectivity and coordination-platform hold all 11 ranked problem patterns.
Scope: Dataset zookeeper, 2015-07-29 to 2015-08-26 (5 weeks), compared with the previous period 2015-07-01 to 2015-07-29. Problem patterns were filtered with problem_filter jev, giving 11 matches. The storage-persistence view was filtered by team. Results were not truncated.
storage-persistence produced 284 log lines out of 74380 in the period, against 59036 for coordination-platform and 15060 for client-connectivity.
All 284 storage-persistence log lines have severity INFO, and there is only 1 severity group for the team.
The storage-persistence patterns have 0 problem lines each. The busiest are 'Snapshotting: <HEX> to <PATH>' (62 log lines, 11 bursts, p_problem 0.019) and 'Reading snapshot <PATH>' (60 log lines, 11 bursts, p_problem 0.02). Both are judged 'not a problem'.
None of the 11 ranked problem patterns belongs to storage-persistence. 7 belong to coordination-platform and 4 to client-connectivity.
Team roll-up: coordination-platform has 7 problem patterns, 35 bursts and 13585 log lines (previous period 0 bursts). client-connectivity has 4 problem patterns, 30 bursts and 1864 log lines (previous period 0 bursts).
1. 'caught end of stream exception' (client connections ending abnormally), judged a network or I/O failure — owner client-connectivity — 18 bursts (previous period 0), 1670 log lines, active 3 weeks, score 89.5 — Decide whether client-connectivity gets the first slot to find the cause of the new end-of-stream bursts.
2. 'Cannot open channel to <N> at election address' (quorum election connection failures), judged a network or I/O failure — owner coordination-platform — 8 bursts (previous period 0), 2584 log lines, active 5 weeks, score 86.4 — Fund coordination-platform to investigate election-channel connectivity. It was present in all 5 weeks.
3. 'Unexpected Exception: ' in NIOServerCnxn, judged a job or application failure — owner client-connectivity — 9 bursts (previous period 0), 27 log lines, active 2 weeks, score 82.7 — Have client-connectivity triage this alongside rank 1, since both sit in the same component.
Hypothesis: The disk and snapshot concern may come from routine snapshot, purge and log-rotation INFO messages rather than real storage faults. Would confirm: Disk-level metrics or alerts for the ZooKeeper hosts, and the specific messages the reporter saw.
Unknown: Cost, downtime and customer impact are not in these logs.
Unknown: Root cause is not established by these logs.
Unknown: ZooKeeper logs carry no node or host, so nodes is 0 and the spread of each pattern across hosts is unknown.
Unknown: Disk-level health (space, latency) outside the log messages cannot be judged from these logs.

Next step: Ask the person who raised the disk and snapshot concern for the specific errors or host alerts they saw. — The logs for 2015-07-29 to 2015-08-26 show only INFO lines for storage-persistence (284 of 284).
Next step: Check disk monitoring for the ZooKeeper hosts for the same period. — The logs cannot show disk health directly.

coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2015-07-29 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'zookeeper' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'zookeeper' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'zookeeper' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND now.problem_lines > 0 AND j.p_problem >= 0.5 ), inputs AS ( SELECT *, round(weeks_active::DOUBLE / 5, 3) AS persistence, round(problem_lines::DOUBLE / lines, 3) AS problem_share, p_problem AS severity_input FROM base ), ranked AS ( SELECT *, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY bursts) AS pr_frequency, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY change) AS pr_trend, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY nodes) AS pr_spread, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY persistence) AS pr_persistence, cume_dist() OVER (ORDER BY severity_input) AS pr_severity FROM inputs ) SELECT *, round(100 * (0.3 * pr_frequency + 0.2 * pr_trend + 0.25 * pr_spread + 0.15 * pr_persistence + 0.1 * pr_severity), 1) AS score FROM ranked ORDER BY score DESC, bursts DESC, pattern_id

Failed card payments look ongoing, not a one-off blip: the 'Visa cache full' error appears in every sampled minute I checked from 00:00 to 00:29. The error is logged by the payment component (payments-team), while the top-ranked patterns are the web-frontend's reports of it, so payments-team is the likely fix owner with web-frontend as a secondary owner.

By median request time, the slowest nova-api endpoint is POST /v<N>/servers (pattern 100034), with p50 0.504 s against 0.26 s for nova-api overall. The single slowest request (max 4.164 s) was on a different endpoint, GET /v<N>/servers/detail with a host filter (pattern 100056).
Scope: openstack dataset, 2017-05-14 00:00:00 → 2017-05-18 00:00:00. Durations are HTTP request time (time: N). The pattern ranking is truncated to the top 20 patterns (min 5 timed lines) and also includes nova-compute lifecycle-step patterns, which I excluded from the endpoint comparison. The search for pattern 100034 covers the whole corpus.
POST /v<N>/servers HTTP/<N> status 202 (pattern 100034) has the highest p50 of the nova-api HTTP patterns: p50 0.504 s, p95 0.648 s, p99 0.765 s, max 1.793 s, over 2065 log lines, error_rate 0.0.
nova-api as a whole: 98733 timed log lines, p50 0.26 s, p95 0.382 s, p99 0.514 s, max 4.164 s, error_rate 0.0001.
The highest single request time, max 4.164 s, belongs to GET /v<N>/servers/detail?all_tenants=True&changes-since=...&host=cp-... (pattern 100056), whose p50 is 0.333 s and p95 0.503 s over 176 log lines.

It occurred in 8 bursts (8 log lines for this message) between 2017-05-16 03:19:45 and 2017-05-17 05:24:15, and the owning team is cloud-compute.
Scope: Dataset openstack, component nova-compute, 2017-05-16 00:00 to 2017-05-18 00:00 (previous period 2017-05-14 00:00 to 2017-05-16 00:00). Bursts are recurrences with a 30-minute gap. Severity ERROR was the main filter. The top_patterns results are not truncated for the burst ranking (7 matches), but the lines-ranked list shows 12 of 27 patterns and the ERROR search shows a 3-row sample of 192 matches. The openstack logs carry no node/host, so node spread is unknown.
In 2017-05-16 to 2017-05-18, nova-compute had 192 ERROR log lines, out of 194 ERROR log lines in total; nova-api had the other 2.
The nova-compute ERROR log lines ran from 2017-05-16 03:19:45.356000 to 2017-05-17 05:24:15.342000.
The message 'InvalidDiskInfo: Disk info file is invalid: qemu-img failed to execute on /var/lib/nova/instances/<UUID>/disk : Unexpected error while running command.' (pattern 100096) has 8 log lines in the corpus, first at 2017-05-16 03:19:45.356000 and last at 2017-05-17 05:24:15.342000.
Pattern 100096 has 8 bursts in the period against 0 in the previous period (change 8), first seen 2017-05-16 03:19:45.356000, weeks active 1, owner team cloud-compute.
The same 8 bursts include the stderr line "qemu-img: Could not open '/var/lib/nova/instances/<UUID>/disk': ... No such file or directory" (pattern 100097, 8 log lines) and 'Error during ComputeManager._run_image_cache_manager_pass' (pattern 100094, 8 log lines); all of these are new in the period (0 bursts previously).
Traceback frames in manager.py _run_image_cache_manager_pass, images.py qemu_img_info, libvirt/driver.py manage_image_cache and libvirt/imagecache.py each show 8 log lines and 8 bursts, with the same first_seen of 2017-05-16 03:19:45.356000.
1. Image cache manager periodic task fails with InvalidDiskInfo: qemu-img cannot open an instance disk file ('No such file or directory'). Investigate first because it is new this period (0 bursts before) and all 8 bursts are ERROR severity. — owner cloud-compute — 8 bursts (previous period 0, change 8); 8 log lines for pattern 100096; first seen 2017-05-16 03:19:45.356000; weeks active 1; nodes unknown (0). — Check whether the instance directories named in the 8 failing lines exist on the compute host, and whether the image cache manager pass is still failing after 2017-05-17 05:24:15.
2. Power-state sync warning: instance count in the database differs from the hypervisor count. Judged 'not a problem' by the pattern model, but it has the most bursts of the WARNING patterns shown. — owner cloud-compute — 19 bursts (previous period 3, change 16); 41 log lines; weeks active 1; p_problem 0.146. — Confirm whether the mismatch is transient, and check whether it lines up with the InvalidDiskInfo bursts.
3. Warning: couldn't obtain the vcpu count from domain, 'cpu affinity is not supported'. — owner cloud-compute — 7 bursts (previous period 1, change 6); 11 log lines; weeks active 1; p_problem 0.731. — Check whether the libvirt/hypervisor configuration supports CPU affinity queries, or whether the warning is expected noise.
4. Warning: 'Unknown base file' in /var/lib/nova/instances/_base, the highest-volume pattern by log lines. — owner cloud-compute — 2789 log lines in 2 bursts (previous period 1, change 1); weeks active 1. — Check whether it relates to the image cache failure, since both concern the image cache area.
Hypothesis: The disk file for an instance may be missing, for example removed or never created, so qemu-img fails when the image cache manager lists backing images. Would confirm: Check on the compute host whether the /var/lib/nova/instances/<UUID>/disk paths in the failing lines exist, and compare the instance UUIDs with the database.
Hypothesis: The 'Unknown base file' and power-state mismatch warnings may share a cause with the image cache failure, such as instance or base-image files being out of sync with the database. Would confirm: Compare the timing of these warning bursts with the 8 ERROR bursts and check the instance state in the database.
Unknown: Which hosts or nodes are affected: the openstack logs carry no node, so spread is unknown.
Unknown: Root cause: the logs show the symptom (qemu-img could not open the disk file) but not why the file is missing.
Unknown: Whether the failure continues after 2017-05-17 05:24:15, since the requested window ends 2017-05-18 00:00 and the last ERROR line in it is at 2017-05-17 05:24:15.342.
Unknown: Customer impact, downtime and cost are not in the logs.
Next step: Inspect the instance directories for the UUIDs in the 8 InvalidDiskInfo lines on the compute host, and run qemu-img info manually on any disk that exists. — The stderr says 'No such file or directory' in all 8 bursts, which points to a missing disk file.
Next step: Pull the log lines around the 8 burst start times, starting with 2017-05-16 03:19:45, to see what precedes each image cache manager pass failure. — The first burst has no earlier occurrence (previous period 0), so what triggered it is unexplained.
Next step: Review the power-state sync warning (19 bursts) and the vcpu affinity warning (7 bursts) to decide whether they are noise or related symptoms. — Both rose against the previous period (changes of 16 and 6).

coalesce(b_prev.bursts_prev, 0) AS change, round(top_node.top_node_lines::DOUBLE / now.lines, 3) AS top_node_share, p.first_ts AS first_seen, p.first_ts >= '2017-05-16 00:00:00' AS new, round(j.p_fault, 3) AS p_fault, round(j.p_dump, 3) AS p_dump, round(j.p_problem, 3) AS p_problem, round(j.p_threat, 3) AS p_threat, j.kind FROM now JOIN patterns p ON p.dataset = 'openstack' AND p.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN pattern_judgments j ON j.dataset = 'openstack' AND j.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN ownership o ON o.dataset = 'openstack' AND o.component = p.component LEFT JOIN top_node ON top_node.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_now ON b_now.pattern_id = now.pattern_id LEFT JOIN b_prev ON b_prev.pattern_id = now.pattern_id WHERE TRUE AND now.problem_lines > 0 AND p.component = 'nova-compute' ) SELECT *, count(*) OVER () AS candidates FROM base ORDER BY lines DESC, pattern_id LIMIT 12
